title: The<scp>CartACom</scp>model: transforming cartographic features into communicating agents for cartographic generalisation
relevance_reason: The paper concerns cartographic generalisation of GIS vector data (geometric features such as points, lines, polygons) using agent-based models; the term 'vector' refers to GIS geometry, not to vector databases or similarity/nearest-neighbor search technology.
research_focus: Automated cartographic generalisation of topographic vector data (GIS geometric features) using a new agent-based model (CARTACOM) that handles relational constraints between map objects in low-density, heterogeneous areas.
method: Agent-based model in which cartographic objects are autonomous agents that perceive their spatial surroundings, communicate with neighbours via predefined dialogue protocols, and autonomously select and apply generalisation algorithms (e.g. elimination, aggregation) to satisfy relational constraints. A hook to the AGENT model is provided for internal constraints.
application_domain: Cartographic generalisation / map production for topographic data
results_summary: The paper presents CARTACOM, an agent-based generalisation model dedicated to relational constraints between cartographic objects in low-density areas. The model was implemented on LAMPS2, Clarity, and the CartAGen research platform. Results on rural topographic data at scales 1:25,000 to 1:50,000 demonstrated successful self-elimination of buildings to satisfy proximity constraints and road generalisation via the AGENT model. The authors conclude the approach is well adapted for heterogeneous, non-hierarchically organised areas where rubber-sheeting alone is insufficient.
limitations: Dedicated only to areas of low density where rubber-sheeting is insufficient; not a general-purpose generalisation model; Focuses on relational constraints; internal constraints require a hook to the separate AGENT model; Applied specifically to rural, non-hierarchically organised areas

title: GEOMETRICAL ADJUSTMENT TOWARDS THE ALIGNMENT OF VECTOR DATABASES
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector databases' in the geospatial/GIS sense (databases containing vector geographic features such as lines and polygons), not in the computer science sense of databases for storing and searching high-dimensional embedding vectors. It addresses geometric alignment of spatial data and has no connection to vector indexing, nearest neighbor search, or vector database technology.
research_focus: The alignment and harmonization of geospatial vector databases (line and polygon features) by resolving local geometric distortions and discrepancies between different spatial data sources using a localized geometric adjustment process.
method: A localized geometric alignment process that exploits local spatial, topologic, and geometric relationships between corresponding line-features, followed by Least Squares Adjustment (LSA) to quantify and resolve local distortions, as opposed to a global affine transformation.
application_domain: Geospatial data alignment, specifically harmonization of cadastral and topographic vector databases
results_summary: The paper demonstrates that the proposed localized geometric alignment process significantly reduces geometric discrepancies (gaps, continuity issues, positional offsets) between different geospatial vector databases. In experiments with cadastral and topographic databases, corresponding features were perfectly aligned after three iterations, with residuals decreasing from approximately 17.98 m² to 0.42 m². A synthetic test using a known affine transformation confirmed that the calculated transformation parameters closely matched the true values, with standard deviations of approximately ±0.1 m. The results suggest a statistically sound and reliable solution for resolving spatial inconsistency between different vector data sources.
limitations: The alignment model has a local fashion, which introduces small standard deviations in calculated parameters compared to a global point-to-point model; In some cases, a mere geometric analysis of possible corresponding features is not successful when several neighboring objects are possible; Poor geometry constellation of data (sparsely distributed points and excessive ones) can cause problems that are not yet fully addressed
research_gaps: Adding more constraints to handle poor geometry constellation (sparsely distributed points and excessive ones); Analyzing larger databases with wider coverage areas and managing the resulting larger normal equation systems; Applying hierarchical partitioning of space (e.g., using major road network as high-level objects) to reduce the number of features involved; Using supplementary data such as semantics, attributes, and topological characteristics to better identify corresponding features for alignment

title: A Vector Data Model for Efficiently Rendering Large Vector Maps on Global 3D Terrain Surfaces
relevance_reason: The paper concerns organizing geographic vector data (map features such as points, lines, polygons) for 3D terrain rendering in GIS; the 'vector database' referenced is a spatial GIS database (ArcSDE, Oracle Spatial), not a vector similarity search database. There is no discussion of embedding-based nearest neighbor search, vector indexing for similarity retrieval, or any vector database technology relevant to the survey.
research_focus: Proposing a Vector Tiled Pyramid Model (VTPM) for organizing geographic vector data (map features) to enable efficient rendering of large vector maps on global 3D terrain surfaces in 3D GIS.
method: A hierarchical tiled pyramid structure in which vector data at different scales are stored as separate levels, each level partitioned into fixed-size vector tiles organized in a grid index, allowing fast access by locating only the relevant tile rather than searching the entire dataset.
application_domain: 3D GIS, geographic map visualization on 3D terrain surfaces
results_summary: The paper proposes the VTPM and validates it through a prototype system for visualizing vector data on 3D terrain surfaces. Experimental results show that, compared with a traditional GIS vector database, the VTPM enables faster access to vector data for rendering on 3D terrain. The efficiency advantage is more pronounced when requesting large-scale (lower-level) vector tiles. Unlike texture tiled pyramids, the VTPM preserves vector data details and supports both geometry-based and texture-based rendering approaches, achieving a better balance between efficiency and visual quality.
limitations: The topology of vector data is undermined due to partitioning into tiles, making spatial analysis of the vector data problematic
research_gaps: Building and incorporating a more extensive indexing structure to preserve topological relationships among vector objects in the VTPM

title: Building a Dynamic, Large-Scale Spatio-temporal Vector Database to Support a National Spatial Data Infrastructure in China
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector database' in the GIS sense (storing geographic vector features such as lines, polygons, and points), not in the sense of vector similarity search or nearest neighbor search for high-dimensional embeddings. It is about spatio-temporal geographic data management and has no connection to vector database technology for ANN search.
research_focus: Development of a dynamic, large-scale spatio-temporal vector database (geographic vector data) to support China's National Spatial Data Infrastructure, addressing data integration, version management, and change detection for heterogeneous geospatial datasets.
method: A version-difference spatio-temporal data model augmented with dynamic relation techniques for data fusion across multiple versions, implemented as a database management platform and data processing system using object-oriented programming.
application_domain: Geospatial data management, national spatial data infrastructure, land use monitoring, environmental monitoring, urban simulation, emergency management, and cadastre management
results_summary: The paper proposes a version-difference spatio-temporal data model and demonstrates it through two experiments: building a National Fundamental Geospatial Information Dynamic Database at 1:250,000 scale (13 GB vector data, 13 map layers) and applying it to the National Land Use Survey. The approach saves up to one-third storage space compared to snapshot models and achieves over 85% accuracy in automated change detection. The system supports dynamic visualization, cross-version data fusion, and routine land information update management. The authors conclude the methodology has significant advantages over traditional spatio-temporal data models for large-scale national geospatial databases.
limitations: Most current spatio-temporal models are only conceptual without concrete implementation; Comprehensive spatio-temporal database solutions are lacking in the field
research_gaps: Temporal query language; Spatio-temporal topology; Spatio-temporal data mining

title: HierLabelNet: A Two-Stage LLMs Framework with Data Augmentation and Label Selection for Geographic Text Classification
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is geographic text classification using LLMs; a semantic vector database is mentioned only as a component tool for filtering the label space, with no specific system, indexing method, or in-depth discussion of vector database technology.
research_focus: Geographic text classification for earth observation data, addressing challenges of data sparsity, class imbalance, semantic ambiguity, and domain-specific terminology using a two-stage LLM framework.
method: A two-stage LLM framework (HierLabelNet) combining LLM-based data augmentation to mitigate data scarcity, a semantic vector database to filter the label space prior to inference, few-shot prompt learning for domain-specific language understanding, and an output alignment mechanism for classification stability.
application_domain: Geographic text classification, earth observation data management, geospatial information retrieval
results_summary: The HierLabelNet framework was evaluated under few-shot settings by varying the number of contextual examples (Q) across multiple LLM architectures. Under extremely low-shot conditions (Q=1), micro-F1 increased by 3.30 percentage points and macro-F1 by 28.85% for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, with similar gains observed for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Cross-model evaluations showed that generative LLMs like the LLaMA3.1 series exhibited greater responsiveness to the framework. However, as Q increased, performance improvements plateaued with marginal gains below 2%, indicating computational bottlenecks in assimilating large volumes of semantic examples. The framework demonstrated higher efficiency and reduced token consumption in the low-Q regime, favorable for real-world deployment.
limitations: Effectiveness is inherently influenced by the capabilities of the underlying embedding models and LLMs; As the number of contextual examples (Q) increases, performance improvements plateau with marginal gains diminishing to below 2%; Current LLM architectures face computational bottlenecks in assimilating large volumes of semantic examples
research_gaps: Constructing higher-quality and larger-scale domain-specific datasets to enable more effective fine-tuning of embedding models and LLMs for EO domain knowledge; Extending the applicability of the framework to multimodal EO data classification scenarios, integrating heterogeneous sources such as images, text, and spatiotemporal data

title: GisGCN: A Visual Graph-Based Framework to Match Geographical Areas through Time
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about geographic area matching using graph neural networks and GIS data; vector databases and similarity search (FAISS, KNN) are used only as a baseline tool and retrieval mechanism, not as the main subject of study.
research_focus: Cross-time matching of geographical areas by representing geographic entities and their spatial relationships as graphs and learning graph embeddings via a Graph Convolutional Network, enabling retrieval of the same area across different time periods from aerial photographs.
method: A Siamese Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) architecture is used to learn compact graph embeddings of geographic entities (nodes) and their spatial relationships (edges). The embeddings are trained with contrastive learning and evaluated via KNN search, compared against a FAISS-based unsupervised feature similarity baseline. A novel cross-time and cross-source graph dataset is created from topographic vector databases.
application_domain: Geospatial data, historical aerial photograph retrieval, GIS-based geographic area matching
results_summary: The paper proposes GisGCN, a GCN-based Siamese architecture that learns graph embeddings of geographic areas for cross-time matching. For same-source data spanning up to 15 years, the method achieves over 50% correct matches (map@5), outperforming the FAISS-based baseline in noise robustness (10% decrease vs. 70% decrease under attribute noise). However, the GCN-based approach is outperformed by the unsupervised FAISS baseline in raw map@5 scores. Cross-source and cross-time matching yields significantly lower performance, indicating the model does not yet generalize well. The authors conclude the approach is a promising new direction but not yet competitive with classical feature-based methods.
limitations: The model does not generalize well to cross-source data; The training procedure is under-specified; The method requires segmentation as a prior step, which is error-prone; Cross-source tests show quite low map@5 values; Graph architecture and network parameters are highly interdependent with no clear trend; The approach is not generalizable enough at the current state
research_gaps: Improve the efficiency of the matching models; Study different matching architectures; Adapt the GCN to handle graphs of different sizes; Apply the model to new application domains; Adopt an attention mechanism in the graph model; Improve the graph representation for better retrieval results; Encode textual features such as toponyms as additional graph nodes; Extend the approach to matching across oblique aerial image sets

title: An Object -Oriented Method for Designing Geographical Information Systems *
relevance_reason: The paper is about object-oriented GIS design methodology; the term 'vector database' appears only in the GIS sense (a schema storing geometric vector features like points and lines), not in the modern sense of vector databases for high-dimensional embedding similarity search. No vector indexing, nearest-neighbor search, or modern vector database technology is discussed.
research_focus: An object-oriented method for analyzing and designing geographical information systems (GIS), including modeling the organizational system context and designing spatial databases with both spatial and thematic data.
method: Object-oriented modeling using OMT notation to represent GIS entities, their spatial and thematic properties, relationships, and behavior; database integration for merging different views; mapping object-oriented database schemas to relational and vector database schemas.
application_domain: Geographical Information Systems (GIS) design and spatial database development
results_summary: The paper introduces an object-oriented method for the full process of analyzing and designing GIS, going beyond prior methods that focused only on database design. It introduces the notion of 'organizational system' to capture the GIS context and identify requirements, entities, and users. The method uses OMT notation to model the application domain and design the spatial database. The main output is a spatial database design plus application programs, with steps for mapping to relational and vector database schemas. The paper positions itself as addressing the gap of scarce GIS-specific development methods in the literature.

title: Remote Sensing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Bridging remote sensing imagery and comprehensive knowledge with a multimodal dataset and retrieval-augmented generation model
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a RAG framework and dataset for remote sensing VLMs; the vector database is used only as an internal retrieval component (encoding into a shared embedding space and top-k retrieval) without any analysis, comparison, or improvement of vector database technology itself.
research_focus: Addressing the limitation of remote sensing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in incorporating external domain and world knowledge by proposing a multimodal dataset (RSWK) and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework (RS-RAG) for knowledge-grounded remote sensing vision-language tasks.
method: Construction of the RSWK multimodal dataset (14,820 satellite images with rich textual descriptions of landmarks across 16 categories and 184 countries) and design of the RS-RAG framework, which includes a Multi-Modal Knowledge Vector Database Construction module (encoding imagery and text into a shared embedding space) and a Knowledge Retrieval and Response Generation module (retrieving, re-ranking, and incorporating knowledge into VLM prompts).
application_domain: Remote sensing and Earth observation: image captioning, image classification, and visual question answering over satellite imagery of globally recognized landmarks
results_summary: The authors constructed the RSWK dataset and the RS-RAG framework, then evaluated performance on three tasks (image captioning, image classification, VQA) against multiple VLM baselines. On image captioning, RS-RAG achieved BLEU-1 of 0.490 and CIDEr of 0.145, outperforming the best baseline (Qwen2.5-VL) by 10.5 and 12.7 points respectively. On image classification, RS-RAG reached an overall accuracy of 0.79 versus 0.61 for the strongest baseline, leading in 13 of 16 categories. On VQA, RS-RAG achieved BLEU-1 of 0.254 and CIDEr of 0.685, surpassing the best baseline (RSGPT) by 4.5 and 11.6 points. Qualitative analyses confirmed RS-RAG's superior ability to correctly identify landmarks and integrate factual and domain-specific knowledge into outputs.
research_gaps: Developing more capable, explainable, and generalizable multimodal systems for Earth observation and related applications

title: GEOSPATIAL DATABASE UPDATING SYSTEM with WMS and DIRECT CONNECTION METHOD
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector database' in the GIS sense (a database storing geographic vector features such as lines, polygons, and points), not in the ML/AI sense of storing high-dimensional embeddings for similarity search. No vector indexing, nearest neighbor search, or vector database technology (e.g., FAISS, HNSW, Milvus) is discussed.
research_focus: Designing an efficient system for updating the Turkish Topographic Vector Database (TOPOVT) using a combination of WMS service for data display and direct database connection for editing, to enable rapid and information-preserving updates of national-scale topographic vector data.
method: A hybrid system combining three components: (1) a WMS service to display data as images at desired scales, (2) a personal vector database on the user side for performing add/update/delete operations, and (3) linking software connecting the WMS publication with the vector data structure. Two independent enterprise database systems with short-interval synchronization provide redundancy.
application_domain: Geospatial data management and topographic mapping (national-scale 3D topographic vector data for Turkey)
results_summary: The paper describes a system designed to update TOPOVT efficiently without losing information content, combining WMS display convenience with WFS-based vector editing capabilities. Two independent enterprise database systems were established with synchronization to ensure the updating process is not affected by system failures. The system allows real-time monitoring of field updates via internet connection and prevents performance slowdown by not directly accessing the vector database for display. The approach enables rapid data entry while preserving topological relationships and historical metadata of updated features.
limitations: The system is developed using ArcGIS libraries (licensed software), which limits accessibility due to high costs; The system is designed for a specific database (TOPOVT) and specific organizational workflow (General Command of Mapping of Turkey)
research_gaps: Application of the proposed system with open-source GIS software (QGIS, SAGA, GRASS) is suggested but not yet implemented; How well web-based systems can respond to the needs of specialized data producers remains an open question

title: GENCP: GAN-Based Ground Control Point Generation for Satellite Image Georeferencing
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector' exclusively in the GIS/geographic sense (vector maps, vector geographic data, vector databases as stores of geographic features) and is fundamentally about GAN-based image generation for satellite georeferencing; it does not address vector databases, vector indexing, or high-dimensional similarity search in any way.
research_focus: Feasibility of using a GAN-based approach (pix2pix) to generate reference image chips from geographic vector data (e.g., OpenStreetMap) for automated satellite image georeferencing and geometric calibration/validation (Cal/Val) workflows.
method: Two pix2pix GAN models were trained to translate rasterized vector map masks into satellite-like image chips at 10 m (Sentinel-2) and 50 cm (WorldView-3, SkySat, Pleiades) resolutions. Generated chips were evaluated via visual inspection, radiometric metrics (PSNR, histogram analysis), and geometric image-matching accuracy using KARIOS.
mentioned_systems: pix2pix; OpenStreetMap; KARIOS; Sentinel-2; WorldView-3; SkySat; Pleiades; Maxar/VANTOR; EDAP; ESA Earthnet; CEOS; Copernicus; GEOSS
application_domain: Remote sensing, satellite image georeferencing, photogrammetry, sensor geometric calibration and validation
results_summary: The study trained two pix2pix GAN models to generate satellite-like image chips from rasterized OpenStreetMap vector data at 10 m and 50 cm resolutions. At VHR (50 cm), generated chips achieved geometric RMSE of approximately 1.5 m (SkySat), 1.6 m (Pleiades), and 2.1 m (Maxar), confirming suitability for automated image matching. At HR (10 m), performance was lower due to abstraction and generalization effects in the vector data. The authors conclude that vector-derived imagery can serve as a scalable, sensor-adaptable reference for Cal/Val workflows, but performance is strongly governed by spatial resolution, vector-image alignment quality, and sensor-specific geometric characteristics.
limitations: Performance is strongly governed by spatial resolution and vector-image alignment quality; Lack of manual content adaptation in the HR dataset limited model performance; Positional accuracy and completeness of OSM were not systematically validated; Sensor-specific factors (off-nadir viewing, roof displacement, DSM limitations, orthorectification quality) influence generated chip quality; Tile size, tile overlap, and semantic mask resolution were not systematically analyzed; Flat RGB mask encoding simplifies the semantic structure of input vector data, removing hierarchical and contextual relations; Absence of temporal, seasonal, and illumination information in the vector domain contributes to radiometric inconsistencies; A controlled ablation analysis of individual preprocessing steps was not performed
research_gaps: Independent assessment of geometric fidelity of target VHR images using surveyed GCPs or other authoritative reference data; Methods for automatically extracting, validating, and ranking reliable GCP candidates from generated chips; Systematic sensitivity analysis of tile size, tile overlap, and semantic mask resolution; Investigation of richer vector representations such as hierarchical semantic classes, multi-channel masks, object attributes, and scale-dependent class generalization; Exploration of hierarchical semantic embedding approaches including hyperbolic feature spaces to preserve semantic distances among vector and land-cover classes; Extension to other sensing modalities including SAR with modality-specific characteristics; Multi-sensor adaptation and automated quality control for full operational deployment
